newsitem.title: UK: Doctors say cancer drug could cause birth defects.
newsitem.headline: Doctors say cancer drug could cause birth defects.

text.p: Doctors in California on Friday reported the case of a baby born with genital defects after her mother took tamoxifen for breast cancer.
They said the case did not mean the popular breast cancer drug caused birth defects, but the possibility bore watching.
Tamerou Asrat and colleagues at Women's Hospital in Long Beach described the case of a 35-year-old woman who became pregnant while taking tamoxifen for recurrent breast cancer.
She had amniocentesis, a common test for possible birth defects, which indicated the baby was a normal girl. She was taken off the drug.
But the woman became very ill and had the baby slightly prematurely. The mother died two weeks later.
"Examination of the infant revealed ambiguous genitalia," Asrat's group wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
"The clitoris was enlarged as a phallic-like structure," they added. Ultrasound revealed the baby had a uterus and ovaries.
Surgery was performed to make her genitals look normal.
Asrat's group noted that tamoxifen had caused some birth defects in rats, but said there had been no trials of the effects of tamoxifen in pregnant women.
"In recent times, more women are delaying pregnancy until later years, and so the number of women of child-bearing age with breast cancer will increase," they wrote.
"It is reasonable to expect an increase in the number of reports of infants exposed to tamoxifen during pregnancy."
Tamoxifen is an anti-oestrogen -- it works against the effects of the female hormone.

It could be that tamoxifen can cause birth defects, they added -- similar to those caused by diethylstilbestrol (DES), a synthetic oestrogen given to women to prevent miscarriage from the mid-1940s until 1971.
Some of the children born to women who took DES looked normal but turned out to be sterile or developed cancers.
There is now a register of people born to women who took DES so that problems can be tracked. Asrat's group suggested the same kind of registry be set up for tamoxifen.
British-based Zeneca Plc is the main manufacturer of tamoxifen.
Wendy Russell, a a spokeswoman for Zeneca, said: "We'll obviously take a note of this."
She said tamoxifen was not supposed to be prescribed to pregnant women, anyway, and the label made this clear.
"Tamoxifen has been available since 1973," she added. "We have well over eight million patient-years experience with this drug."
She said "a small number" of birth defects had been reported and the company was tracking this, as it did with all drugs, but there was no strong evidence that tamoxifen caused birth defects.
